subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra suggested merging memcpy and rep_movs_alternative, as it makes little sense to maintain divergent copies of similar code.
reviews.raw_body:
So no real objection to these patches from me.

However, it did remind me of something I have on the TODO list for a
rainy afternoon, namely merge memcpy and rep_movs_alternative.

It makes very little sense to me that we have two (divergent) copies of
what is basically the same thing.

reviews.author: Borislav Petkov
reviews.summary: Reviewer Borislav Petkov expressed strong disagreement (CONTENTIOUS) with the patch, arguing that it adds unnecessary complexity and makes the code 'unmaintainable' by introducing more JMPs in conditional alternatives. He suggested using alternative_call* or a static key to avoid duplicated code, but rejected the current approach.
reviews.raw_body:
Sorry, this is adding more JMPs in "conditional" alternatives code and thus
turns this into a bigger and unmaintainable mess than it already is.

The 2K limit looks like something conjured out of a thin air as it seems it
work for your particular case. I'm sure we will have to whack it in the future
because someone else will complain of the opposite.

This needs to be done with alternative_call*, even at the price of some
duplicated code but without turning what already is a mess, into a bigger one.

Or a static key or even with stop_machine_nmi() (currently in review) which
patches the kernel even later, when it is convenient to do so.

Whatever it takes to keep this code readable and sane.

But not this.

Sorry.

-- 
Regards/Gruss,
    Boris.

https://people.kernel.org/tglx/notes-about-netiquette

2026-11-11.patch_summary: This patch modifies the x86 memcpy() function to use REP MOVSB for large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM, improving performance by up to 66.8% in certain scenarios. The change involves adding an alternative instruction sequence that uses REP MOVSB when the copy size is 2048 bytes or larger, while keeping the scalar loop for smaller copies. This approach takes into account the specific characteristics of ERMS CPUs and their lack of FSRM support.

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch does not handle the case where the length is less than or equal to 2047 bytes on ERMS CPUs, and suggested adding a check for this condition.

Reviewer suggested using a non-standard calling convention to patch the call sites with 'rep movsb; nop3' and proposed creating a special function for this purpose, also suggesting that a similar approach could be applied to memmove().
reviews.raw_body:
On Wed, 11 Nov 2026 15:46:08 -0800
Borislav Petkov <bp@alien8.de> wrote:

---

Multiple functions seems like a good idea.

In some cases you can patch the constant in the instruction.
That is safe here even if a multi-byte constant crosses a cache line
because it is only an optimisation.

Patching the call sites would certainly be cleaner.
More interesting would be having a function with a non-standard calling
convention (%rdi, %rsi, %rcx, everything else preserved, void result)
so that the 5 byte call can be patched with "rep movsb; nop3".
I can't see anywhere that uses the result.
Maybe start with "rep movsb; nop3" and patch with the call?
You'd still need a normal memcpy() for the calls gcc makes and if the
address is taken.

A special function to do the patching would also make sense.
All Intel non-atom cpu since sandy bridge run 'rep movsb' as fast
as 'rep movsq' - so you only need to worry about short copies.
Whereas some of the older Zen cpu run misaligned copies slowly.
So you could pick/patch the most appropriate code using more complex
logic than just whether one of the X86_FEATURE_xxx bits is set.

The same calling convention might make sense for memmove().
Although it probably wants a scratch register for the (dst - src < len)
check (it might want dst in the scratch register!).

David

2026-11-12.patch_summary: This patch modifies the x86 memcpy() function to use REP MOVSB for large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM, improving performance by up to 66.8% in certain scenarios. The change involves adding an alternative instruction sequence that uses REP MOVSB when the copy size is 2048 bytes or larger, while keeping the scalar loop for smaller copies. This approach takes into account the specific characteristics of ERMS CPUs and their lack of FSRM support.

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary:
Author suggests an alternative implementation to improve maintainability, asking if it's acceptable

Author acknowledged that the threshold of 2048 bytes was chosen based on experiments and explained that changing this value to 32 bytes resulted in slower performance for aligned copies of certain sizes, suggesting that a fix is needed but not specifying one.

Author responded to feedback about adding a CALL/RET pair for every path, including FSRM, by trying an alternative approach using tail jumps to keep REP inline on FSRM CPUs.

Author acknowledged the need for a more maintainable patch and provided an updated version in response to reviewer feedback.
reviews.raw_body:
How about something like what I have added at the end, would that be more
acceptable in terms of maintainability?

---

As mentioned in the commit message as well as [1], 2K came from experiments.

Changing the cmp immediate from 2048 to 32 bytes made aligned warmed
32/64/128/256-byte copies 101.2%/69.5%/53.5%/16.5% slower.

This is usecase driven, as Linus said in [2]: "let's see if somebody finds a
case where the kernel memory copies also care".

If someone finds a case where less than 2K is used and it doesnt cause a
regression for CPUs, they can try lowering it.

---

I tried alternative_call_2() from a C entry with separate helpers. It
adds a helper CALL/RET to every path, including FSRM. The attached
version uses tail jumps, so each helper returns directly to the original
caller and FSRM keeps REP inline. I am hoping this is acceptable?

---

No worries! Hopefully the version below is more maintainable and acceptable
for everyone?

Thanks for the review!
Usama

[1] https://lore.kernel.org/all/20261017192727.2760919-1-usama.arif@linux.dev/
[2] https://git.kernel.org/linus/47ee3f1dd93bcbe031539b1ecdaafb44b661c772

diff --git a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
index 7bb146c811029..8a398edf6e160 100644
--- a/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
+++ b/arch/x86/lib/memcpy_64.S
@@ -27,15 +27,15 @@
  *
  * The 'rep movsb' itself is small enough to replace the call, but the
  * two register moves blow up the code. And one of them is "needed"
- * only for the return value that is the same as the source input,
+ * only for the return value that is the same as the destination input,
  * which the compiler could/should do much better anyway.
  */
 SYM_TYPED_FUNC_START(__memcpy)
-       ALTERNATIVE "jmp memcpy_orig", "", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
-
        movq %rdi, %rax
        movq %rdx, %rcx
-       rep movsb
+       /* FSRM takes precedence. Keep RET outside replacements for ITS. */
+       ALTERNATIVE_2 "jmp memcpy_orig", "jmp memcpy_erms", \
+                     X86_FEATURE_ERMS, "rep movsb", X86_FEATURE_FSRM
        RET
 SYM_FUNC_END(__memcpy)
 EXPORT_SYMBOL(__memcpy)
@@ -44,10 +44,15 @@ SYM_FUNC_ALIAS_MEMFUNC(memcpy, __memcpy)
 SYM_PIC_ALIAS(memcpy)
 EXPORT_SYMBOL(memcpy)

-SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
-       movq %rdi, %rax
-       movq %rdx, %rcx
+/* The entry prepares RAX as the return value and RCX as the count. */
+SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_erms)
+       cmpq $2048, %rcx
+       jb memcpy_orig
+       rep movsb
+       RET
+SYM_FUNC_END(memcpy_erms)

+SYM_FUNC_START_LOCAL(memcpy_orig)
        cmpq $0x20, %rcx
        jb .Lhandle_tail

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary:
Author suggests deferring the introduction of REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM until a specific use case is identified, indicating that no fix is planned at this time.

Author acknowledges a potential issue with replacing the CALL instruction in __memcpy() with REP MOVSB, but explains it's not as simple as just patching the caller's code; instead, they propose adding a helper call and return to handle the existing public ABI.

Author agrees that CPU model and alignment can inform a better policy, but suggests going ahead with the current approach in the patch and refining it later based on further testing or user feedback.
reviews.raw_body:
I think it might be a good idea to start with just a constant and if
someone can comeup with a usecase that needs it patched, we can then
look at this? Basically prefer to keep it usecase driven.

---

Replacing the caller's CALL with REP MOVSB could remove actual call
overhead. The C wrapper I tried patches a CALL inside __memcpy() and
adds a helper call and return. The attached tail dispatcher handles the
existing public ABI and leaves caller-side patching for a follow-up.

The scalar helper currently uses RDX and R8-R11 as scratch. Your private
void interface would need an implementation that preserves those
registers, or register saves. RCX already holds the count, and the
scalar helper preserves RAX and the callee-saved registers.

There are return-value users: memdup_buf() in
lib/crypto/tests/test-utils.h returns memcpy()'s pointer. The normal
entry must still return the original destination in RAX and support
compiler-generated and address-taken calls, as you point out. The
current revision preserves that ABI and its aliases.

---

I agree that CPU model and alignment can inform a better policy.

I think to do this, we need access to many different CPUs to test.
I am confident that the 2K cmp will not regress other CPUs and is a good
start. Would it make sense to go ahead with the apprach in the current
patch and develop later on it if someone comes up with a usecase?

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the patch does not handle the case where the length is exactly 2048 bytes, which would cause a misaligned shift operation in the ERMS alternative.

Reviewer David Laight suggested an alternative implementation of memcpy() that uses REP MOVSB on all CPUs, including ERMS and FSRM, by using inline assembly to create a jump table for different copy sizes and handling misaligned pointers.
sentiment_signals: patch needs additional handling for specific edge case
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 13 Nov 2026 06:11:36 -0800
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

I was thinking more of something like:
(written in the email so untested)

static always_inline void *memcpy(void *dst, const void *src, size_t len)
{
	void *orig_dst = dst;

	asm volatile(	".pushsection ".memcpy_calls\n"
			"\t.long . - 1f\n"
			".popsection\n"
			"1:\trep movsb\n"
			"\tnop; nop"
			: "+c (len), "+D" (dst), "+S" (src)
			:: ASM_CALL_CONSTRAINT);

	return orig_dst;
}

An unused return value will be optimised away at all the call sites.

That will work (maybe slowly) on all cpu.
Then some code reads all the addresses from .memcpy_calls and, if necessary,
patches the 5 bytes to a call to the appropriate function.

It might be worth giving the code one or two scratch registers so that
a short copy loop doesn't need to spill to stack (perhaps %rax and %rdx).
It'll matter less for a longer copy loop.

So you might have:
_memcpy_erms:
	cmp $nnnn, %rcx
	jb  _memcpy_words
	rep movsb
	RET

_memcpy_words:
	cmpb $nnnn %rcx
	jb  _memcpy_bytes
	mov %rax,%rcx
	or  %rcx,%rdi
	or  %rcx,%rsi
	test $7,%rcx
	jnz _memcpy_misaligned
	sub $8,%rax
1:	mov %rcx,[%rsi]
	mov %rdx,8[%rsi]
	mov [%rdi],%rcx
	mov 8[%rdi],%rdx
	add $16,%rdi
	add $16,%rsi
	sub $16,%rax
	jnc 1b:
	jz  2f
	mov %rax,[%si]
	mov [%rdi]%rax]
2:	RET

That isn't the best 2-word loop by any means.
And you may not care about misaligned pointers.
	
etc

David

reviews.author: Linus Torvalds
reviews.summary: Linus Torvalds pointed out that many memcpy() calls are not actual function calls on a C level and that the compiler should be relied upon to optimize small memcpy() calls into loads and stores, making it inefficient to hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for performance reasons.
reviews.raw_body:
The problem with this approach two-fold:

 - many memcpy() calls aren't actually memcpy() calls on a C level

 - many memcpy() that *are* calls on a C level should never be calls
in the generated code

That first case is for things like structure copies etc. And it's
common, and it's important, although for the kernel it's usually a
non-issue because it's *typicay* a small constant-sized copy, which
brings us to the second case...

The second case is hugely important. The compiler needs to turn small
memcpy() calls into just loads and stores. Calling "memcpy()" for a
known 64-byte copy is hugely inefficient.

We used to - long ago - do that "constant small sizes" thing by hand.
It was a huge pain. We now rely on the compiler to do it.

End result: we must *not* hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for
performance reasons, and we cannot catch all cases anyway because the
compiler generates implicit memcpy calls.

This is why I really wish we had the compiler just generate a
different sequence for 'call memcpy'. One that used a different
callign convention - preferably just the 'rep movs' one so that we
could just rewrite the call with 'rep movsb' in place.

Without compiler support, we're kind of screwed.

              Linus

              Linus

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer noted that the patch does not handle the case where the length is less than 2048 bytes correctly, as it uses REP MOVSB for lengths greater than or equal to 2048 bytes without considering the ERMS feature.

Reviewer suggested using a small-constant-size threshold to detect when to use the scalar loop instead of REP MOVSB, allowing the compiler to potentially inline smaller copies

The reviewer expressed frustration that the patch does not address non-standard calling conventions in other functions, citing an example where a jump table optimization requires spilling to the stack.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 13 Nov 2026 09:34:26 -0800
Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org> wrote:

---

Actually you could detect the 'small constant sizes' and call the real
memcpy for them.
The compiler would then (hopefully) inline them as a series of moves.

---

I knew you had wished that in the past.
It isn't as though it doesn't have other calls with (annoying)
non-standard calling conventions.
For one arch we optimise 'shift by count' with a jump table, and fall
foul of needing a scratch register - so have to spill to stack.

David
